title: Nirmala learning
hookLine: Nirmala scholars wrote commentaries explaining Gurbani

lines: SOUNDS GOOD: A YES, OR A SIGH?
ONE WORD CAN LEAN TWO WAYS.
cards: Two people read the same text message. Sounds good. One hears a happy yes.
The other hears a tired, flat, fine, whatever. Same two words, two meanings, and the difference lives in something the words don't show. Old texts can do this too, Gurbani among them.

A single word can lean two ways. So, for a long time, people have sat down with the Guru's lines and written out, slowly, what each one means. A scholar's explanation like that has a name, and Nirmala scholars wrote them.

teach.b: The name is teeka: a commentary that walks through a text line by line. A teeka sets out the Guru's line, then the meaning of its words, then what the line is doing, and sometimes other ways to read it.
Nirmala scholars wrote teekas and gave spoken explanations called katha, and students of Gurbani have learned from them. Here's the kind of question they worked on.
The Japji's first step opens with a line built on the word soch. In paraphrase: by soch, it cannot be reached, even if one does soch a hundred thousand times.
Soch can mean thinking; read that way, you can't think your way to God, however hard you think.
But soch can also mean ritual cleansing, the bath and washing some held made a person pure; read that way, outward washing, however often, can't make the mind clean.
Some readers hear it one way, some the other, and some hold both at once. Notice the link to yesterday's word, nirmal, without stain: either reading is about what actually makes a person clear.

teach.h: A CAREFUL TEEKA LISTS THE READINGS.
teach.b: A careful teeka is honest when a word is hard, and lists the readings instead of hiding the choice. And it never replaces the Guru's line.
The line stays on top; the explanation sits underneath.
Readers can disagree with a teeka; that's allowed, and part of the tradition. The point of explaining is to send the reader back to the line with better ears.

how: Sikhs study Gurbani with teekas, written line-by-line commentaries, and katha, spoken explanation in the gurdwara; Nirmala scholars are among those who wrote and taught them.

o: a rule against explaining Gurbani in public

games.q: inside Nirmala learning: tap the pairs.

games.q: you're writing a teeka, and you reach a word that can be read two ways. what does a careful commentator do?
o: pick one and hide the other.
list the readings and let the reader see the choice.
games.why: a careful teeka lists the readings, the way readers of the Japji set out both senses of soch.

practice: Hold the Japji's line in mind: by soch, it cannot be reached. On one breath hear it as thinking, you can't think your way there; on the next, as washing, outward cleaning can't clean the mind.
Go back and forth slowly, and let both readings stand.
